fixes.explanation: Verse 32 says Evil-merodach, the king of Babylon, "…spoke kindly to Jehoiachin…" Kindly, friend. After a pardon and an open prison door, the king's words are kind too. That's a good turn in this chapter.

Not quite. Verse 33 says Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes, and "…he dined regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life." The prison clothes are gone. A seat at the king's table is where the text puts him.

Verse 2 doesn't dance around it. Zedekiah, the king of Judah, "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done." Jehoiakim was an earlier king of Judah. Crown on his head, throne under him, and that's the verdict. The chapter tells you early what kind of story this is.

I'd love to hand you a cleanup scene, friend, but verse 2 doesn't have one. It says Zedekiah, Judah's king, "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done." Jehoiakim was an earlier king of Judah. Nothing about idols coming down. That would be a very different chapter.

Not in this verse. Verse 2 says Zedekiah, the king of Judah, "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, just as Jehoiakim had done." Jehoiakim was an earlier king of Judah. No scaffolding, no work crew, no ribbon cutting. The text puts it in one plain line.

Verse 4 says Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, "…encamped outside the city and built a siege wall all around it." All around, friend. Jerusalem was ringed in. Then verse 5 says the city was kept under siege until Zedekiah's eleventh year.

A trench isn't what verse 4 says. The army of Nebuchadnezzar, Babylon's king, "…built a siege wall all around it." Wall, not trench. The text is specific on this one, and the siege that followed was a hard time for the city.

That's not what verse 7 says. The text says "…all the men of war fled the city by night…" They went out through the gate between the two walls near the king's garden. Surrender isn't in the verse, friend. Fleeing is.
Verse 11 says the king of Babylon took Zedekiah to Babylon, "…where he kept him in custody until his dying day." It's a heavy verse. I think this one hurts. Let's sit with it for a moment.

Verse 13 says otherwise. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, "…burned down the house of the LORD, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem—every significant building." The palace and the houses are on that list. They were burned down, friend.

Not so, friend. Verse 15 says Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, "…carried into exile…" some of the poorest people and those who remained in the city. Verse 16 says he left behind some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and fields. It wasn't a free-for-all.
